reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / paediatric hepatology reference texts
clinicalPearls: An abnormal communication that diverts portal blood into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver, classified as extrahepatic (Abernethy) or intrahepatic
Abernethy type 1 has complete diversion with absent intrahepatic portal supply, whereas type 2 preserves some portal perfusion via a side-to-side shunt
May be detected antenatally, in the neonate with cholestasis or galactosaemia-like screening abnormalities, or later with hepatic encephalopathy
Loss of hepatic first-pass metabolism leads to hyperammonaemia and neurocognitive symptoms, and pulmonary complications such as hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension can occur
Benign and malignant liver nodules, including focal nodular hyperplasia-like lesions and hepatocellular tumours, arise because of the altered hepatic perfusion
Frequently associated with congenital heart disease and other anomalies, prompting a search for coexisting malformations
Management ranges from shunt closure by embolisation or surgical ligation when intrahepatic portal vasculature can recruit, to transplantation for type-1 lesions
reference.pathophysiology: A congenital portosystemic shunt is a developmental anomaly of the portal venous system in which portal blood is shunted directly into a systemic vein, partially or completely bypassing hepatic sinusoidal metabolism. Diversion of nutrient- and hormone-rich portal blood deprives the liver of trophic and metabolic exposure, producing hyperammonaemia, deranged bile-acid and galactose handling, and abnormal vasoactive-substance clearance that predisposes to hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension. Altered intrahepatic haemodynamics also promote the formation of regenerative and neoplastic liver nodules.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired portosystemic collaterals from portal hypertension
Urea-cycle or other inherited metabolic causes of hyperammonaemia
Hepatopulmonary syndrome from chronic liver disease
Focal nodular hyperplasia or hepatocellular tumours of other aetiology
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound to identify the shunt and assess intrahepatic portal flow
Contrast-enhanced CT or MR angiography to define shunt anatomy and classify the malformation
Echocardiography and evaluation for associated cardiac and other anomalies
Cross-sectional imaging surveillance for liver nodules
Assessment for hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension
redFlags: Progressive hepatic encephalopathy or marked hyperammonaemia
Hypoxaemia from hepatopulmonary syndrome or signs of portopulmonary hypertension
Development or growth of hepatic nodules suggesting malignant change
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on shunt type and complications; many type-2 and intrahepatic shunts do well after closure with recruitment of the portal system, whereas type-1 lesions with absent portal supply may ultimately require liver transplantation.
pitfalls: Attributing hyperammonaemia solely to a metabolic disorder and missing the vascular anomaly
Closing a shunt without confirming that the intrahepatic portal vasculature can accommodate restored flow
Assuming a liver nodule is benign without surveillance for malignant transformation
Overlooking associated cardiac and pulmonary complications
